g12-history-uh3-t1.overview: In the nineteenth century long distance caravan trade linked the interior of Ethiopia to the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden and brought the peoples of the north and the south into steady contact. This lesson follows the routes, market centres, trade items and merchants of that trade and explains how it drew Ethiopians together.
objectives: Identify the main trade routes and market centres of the nineteenth century long distance trade
Name the principal export commodities, including ivory, civet, gold, wax, skins and slaves
Explain the factors that revived long distance trade at the beginning of the nineteenth century
Describe the role of the Jabarti and the Afkala merchants in the caravan trade
Explain how long distance trade promoted the interaction of the Ethiopian peoples
g12-history-uh3-t1.simple: Long distance trade is the exchange of goods between distant places along caravan routes. In nineteenth century Ethiopia it revived partly because five Oromo kingdoms rose in the Gibe region and because the Egyptian conquest of South Arabia improved order along the Red Sea coast. Caravans carried ivory, civet, gold, wax, animal skins and slaves from the south, and by the last quarter of the century coffee too. The main routes began at Bonga in Kafa and the Gibe region and passed through Jimma, Saka, Assendabo, Basso and Gondar, or through Soddo and Ankober to Harar and the ports of Zeila and Berbera. Muslim merchants, the northern Jabarti and the southwestern Afkala, led the trade. Along the routes goods, ideas, Islam and culture moved between peoples.
g12-history-uh3-t1.detailed:
What long distance trade was. Long distance trade was the exchange of goods between far apart regions along caravan routes. In nineteenth century Ethiopia it linked the natural wealth of the south and southwest with the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden. It differed from ordinary local trade because caravans travelled for weeks through many market centres controlled by different lords before reaching the coast.

Why the trade revived. The establishment of a monarchical system among the southwestern Oromo regions, particularly the rise of the five Oromo kingdoms in the Gibe region, was one factor that revived the long distance trade and brought back northern Ethiopian merchants to the Gibe region. Although the early nineteenth century was disturbed by regional feudal wars, the relative improvement of political conditions along the Red Sea coast after the Egyptian conquest of South Arabia strengthened peace and order and raised the importance of the Red Sea as a channel of trade.

The routes and market centres. One main caravan route started from the Gibe region and led to Assendabo in Guduru in eastern Wollega, a market that served as a point of contact between the Abay and the Gibe river valleys. From Assendabo goods reached Basso in Gojjam, north of the Abay River, where Muslim and Christian merchants from Tigray, Gondar, Wollo, Shewa and Oromia met. From Basso merchants went to Derita in Begemder and then to Gondar, where the route divided to the Sudan through Metemma and to Massawa through Adwa. Shewa merchants went on to Ankober, while Wollo merchants went to Aussa and the ports of Tajura and Obock. Bati and Ancharo were important market centres in Wollo. A second line from the Gibe region ran north-east to the Soddo market in Gurage land and on to Ankober, and with the rise of the Shewan kingdom the route linking the Shewan plateau with Harar revived, ending at Zeila or Berbera.

The principal caravan routes. The textbook lists three main lines: Bonga in Kafa to Jimma, Saka, Assendabo, Basso and Gondar, which then branched to the Sudan through Metemma or to Massawa through Adwa; Bonga to Jimma, Saka, Assendabo, Aussa and the ports of Tajura and Obock; and Bonga to Jimma, Soddo, Ankober and Harar, ending at Zeila or Berbera.

Trade items and the slave trade. Throughout the nineteenth century the major trading items were ivory, civet, gold, wax, animal skins and slaves. By the last quarter of the century coffee also became an important export. Ethiopian exports were natural products obtained mainly from southwestern Ethiopia. Slaves had been a major export since ancient times and were sent to the Sudan and Arabia; the well known slave auction markets were Yejjube in Gojjam and Abdul Rasul near Aleyu Amba. Coffee grew in importance especially after rail transport in the twentieth century made it possible to move it in large quantities.

The merchants. Although there were some Christian merchants, most traders were Muslim merchants from northern Ethiopia known as Jabarti. They travelled in large caravans and chose a head called Negade Ras, a term later transformed into Negadras. The Afkala, the dominant Muslim merchants of southwestern Ethiopia, came to dominate the local trade of the Gibe region. The Jabarti kept a dominant role in the long distance trade until they faced competition from the Afkala, who had connections along the caravan routes and better protection from local people; by the middle of the nineteenth century most caravan trade between the south and northern Ethiopia was conducted by the Afkala.

Trade as a factor for people's interaction. The revival of long distance trade shaped politics in the Gibe region. Through the agency of Muslim merchants Islam was introduced to the Gibe region in the first half of the nineteenth century, and it helped the Oromo chiefs to establish monarchies and legitimise their power by setting aside the Gada system and other practices opposed to hereditary rule. Islam also helped rulers strengthen the state, reinforce their authority and expand trade. The trade created strong links between the peoples of northern and southwestern Ethiopia, whose merchants began to intermingle, and there was an exchange of ideas and cultures.

workedExamples.problem: Using the caravan routes, explain how ivory from the Gibe region could reach both the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden.
workedExamples.given: The routes began in the south and ran through Assendabo and Basso; one branch went through Derita to Gondar and then to Massawa, while another passed through Soddo and Ankober to Harar and then to Zeila or Berbera.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: a trade route is a chain of market centres that links a producing interior to a distant coast.
workedExamples.substitution: Tracing the chains gives Gibe, Assendabo, Basso, Derita, Gondar, Adwa and Massawa, and Gibe, Assendabo, Soddo, Ankober, Harar, Zeila or Berbera.
workedExamples.calculation: Because each chain ends at a different sea, the same goods could leave through two separate coasts.
workedExamples.answer: Gibe goods reached the Red Sea through Massawa and the Gulf of Aden through Zeila or Berbera.

workedExamples.problem: Why did Islam spread in the Gibe region in the first half of the nineteenth century?
workedExamples.given: Muslim merchants conducted the caravan trade, and the Oromo chiefs were building monarchies.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: trade carries ideas and religion along with goods.
workedExamples.substitution: The merchants who controlled the trade also introduced Islam, and the chiefs saw in it a way to legitimise hereditary rule.
workedExamples.calculation: Islam helped the chiefs set aside the Gada system, strengthen the state and expand trade, so it spread together with the trade.
workedExamples.answer: Islam spread because Muslim merchants brought it with the caravan trade, and the Oromo chiefs used it to legitimise monarchy and strengthen their states.

workedExamples.problem: Compare the position of the Jabarti and the Afkala in the trade by the middle of the nineteenth century.
workedExamples.given: The Jabarti were northern Muslim merchants who kept a monopoly, while the Afkala were dominant Muslim merchants of southwestern Ethiopia with connections along the routes.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: control of a trade route depends on connections, protection and access to goods.
workedExamples.substitution: The Afkala had better protection from local people and could travel safely between the market places of the north and the Gibe region.
workedExamples.calculation: These advantages let the Afkala take over most of the caravan trade between the south and northern Ethiopia.
workedExamples.answer: By the middle of the century the Jabarti still held a monopoly, but most caravan trade between the south and northern Ethiopia was conducted by the Afkala.

workedExamples.problem: Why did long distance trade revive in the early nineteenth century even though regional feudal wars were continuing?
workedExamples.given: There were intense regional feudal wars, yet political conditions along the Red Sea coast improved after the Egyptian conquest of South Arabia.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: trade needs reasonably safe routes, so peace at key outlets can outweigh disorder elsewhere.
workedExamples.substitution: Improved peace and order along the Red Sea coast raised the importance of the Red Sea as a channel of trade.
workedExamples.calculation: Because the coastal outlets became more secure, the caravan trade from the interior could restart and grow.
workedExamples.answer: The revival was helped by the new Oromo monarchies of the Gibe region, which reconnected the north with the south, and by improved peace and order along the Red Sea coast.

g12-history-uh3-t1.summary: Nineteenth century long distance trade revived with the rise of the Oromo kingdoms in the Gibe region and improved order along the Red Sea coast. Caravans carried ivory, civet, gold, wax, animal skins, slaves and later coffee along routes that began at Bonga and the Gibe region and ended at Massawa, Tajura, Obock, Zeila and Berbera. Muslim merchants, above all the Jabarti and the Afkala, led the trade, which spread Islam in the Gibe region and created lasting links and cultural exchange between the peoples of northern and southwestern Ethiopia.

g12-history-uh3-t2.overview: Between 1769 and 1855 the Zemene Mesafint left Ethiopia divided among regional lords while the Orthodox Church was torn by doctrinal disputes. This lesson follows Kassa Hailu's rise as Tewodros II, the reigns of Tewodros II and Yohannis IV, and the shift of the political centre to Shewa under Menilek II.
objectives: Explain how the Zemene Mesafint weakened the central government and the Orthodox Church
Describe the four battles by which Kassa Hailu ended the Era of Princes
Assess the reforms and the downfall of Emperor Tewodros II
Explain how Emperor Yohannis IV governed his vassals and defended Ethiopia
Describe the shift of the political centre from the north to Shewa under Menilek II
g12-history-uh3-t2.simple: The Zemene Mesafint, or Era of Princes, lasted from 1769 to 1855. The Solomonic kings were weak, the Yejju or Worashe lords dominated politics from Debre Tabor, and the Orthodox Church was divided by disputes about the birth of Christ. Peasants suffered most from constant civil war. Kassa Hailu defeated the regional lords at Guramba in 1852, Gorgora Bichen in 1853, Ayshal in June 1853 and Deresge in February 1855, and was crowned Tewodros II. He tried to unify the country, build a national army and make firearms at Gafat, but he clashed with the church and the lords and took his own life at Meqdela in 1868. Yohannis IV ruled from 1872 to 1889 with a liberal system, and Menilek II then moved the political centre to Shewa.
g12-history-uh3-t2.detailed:
The Zemene Mesafint. From 1769 to the middle of the nineteenth century Ethiopia experienced intense regionalism. The country was divided into several almost independent regional polities, which were themselves divided into smaller units, and the power of the so-called Solomonic kings was thoroughly weakened. The Yejju Rases, also known as the Worashe, were Amharised Oromos with a Muslim background who dominated Ethiopian politics from 1769 to 1855. They took the title Ras Bitwoded and most of them used Debre Tabor as their capital, but they could not bring lasting peace and unity.

Religious doctrinal controversies. Christianity was introduced in Ethiopia in the fourth century AD, and the first and dominant sect was the Orthodox sect. In the medieval period there was a dispute between the House of Abba Ewostatewos and the House of Teklehaimanot over the observance of Saturday as a Sabbath, resolved by Emperor Zera Yacob in 1450 at the Council of Debre Metmaq, which accepted both Saturday and Sunday as holy days. During the Zemene Mesafint new disputes arose over the birth of Christ: one group claimed three births (Soset Ledet) while the other claimed two births (Hulet Ledet), also called Karra. Emperor Yohannis IV supported the Hulet Ledet group. The Qebat or Unction doctrine was strong in Gojjam, Ye Tsega Lej or Grace was dominant first in Gondar and then in Shewa, and the Tewahedo or Union doctrine, supported by the Egyptian Patriarch, was dominant in much of Tigray and Lasta. Because these divisions had a regional character, they prevented the Church from playing its traditional role as a cohesive institution.

The plight of the peasants. The Zemene Mesafint was marked by frequent civil wars among regional lords, and the peasants were the principal victims. They were forced to attend battles against their will and to hand over their produce to the lords near them. They paid numerous taxes to numerous lords and had to feed and care for soldiers assigned to them through the billeting system, because the soldiers were not salaried. Because of the constant wars they could not farm in peace. Yet the period was not complete anarchy: there were times of relative peace, and the Yejju lords helped the weakened monarchy survive.

The rise of Tewodros II. To reunite the country a young man named Kassa Hailu rose against the Worashe dynasty. In November 1852 he defeated Dejach Goshu Zewde of Gojjam at the battle of Guramba. In April 1853 he routed the vassals of Ras Ali Alula, including Dejach Birru Goshu and Dejach Birru Aligaz, at the battle of Gorgora Bichen. On 29 June 1853 he defeated Ras Ali Alula at the battle of Ayshal, which put an end to Worashe rule. The last obstacle, Dejach Wube Haile Mariam of Simen, was defeated at Deresge in February 1855, and Kassa Hailu ascended the throne as Tewodros II, King of Kings of Ethiopia. The battle of Deresge brought an end to the Zemene Mesafint.

Reforms and fall of Tewodros II. Tewodros II tried to unify the country, introduce a centralised administration and create a national army to prepare for foreign, especially Egyptian, aggression. After his defeat at the battle of Deberki in 1848 he came to value military training, discipline and good firearms, and he introduced military titles such as Aser Aleqa, Hamsa Aleqa, Meto Aleqa and Shaleqa. He quarrelled with the clergy and the patriarch Abune Selama not for religious reasons but because he tried to take the extra land holdings of the church to give to landless peasants; Abune Selama excommunicated him, and Tewodros imprisoned the Abune in 1864. The Abune died in prison in 1867. He also asked Queen Victoria of England for skilled personnel to make firearms in Ethiopia, and when no quick reply came he detained the British consul Captain Cameron and European missionaries and forced them to make mortars at the gun foundry at Gafat near Debre Tabor, the largest being named Sevastopol. In 1867 Britain sent an expedition under General Robert Napier. On 10 April 1868 the British routed the Ethiopian forces at the battle of Arogee, where Fitawrari Gebreye was killed, and stormed Meqdela. Tewodros released the European hostages and took his own life on 13 April 1868 rather than surrender.

Yohannis IV and the shift to Shewa. After the death of Tewodros three lords sought the throne: Dejazmach Kassa Mircha of Tigray, Wagshum Gobezie Gebre Medhin of Lasta and Menilek Haile Melekot of Shewa. Gobezie ruled first as Emperor Tekle Giorgis for less than three years, and in July 1871 Kassa Mircha defeated and captured him at the battle of Asem, helped by modern weapons he had received from General Napier. In 1872 Kassa Mircha became Emperor Yohannis IV and ruled until 1889. He was politically liberal and followed an administration that resembled federalism, granting a great deal of autonomy to regional and dynastic rulers. In 1878 he forced Menilek of Shewa to drop the title king of kings and confirmed him king of Shewa, and in 1881 he designated Ras Adal Tesema of Gojjam as Negus of Gojjam and Kafa. Yohannis IV devoted most of his time to defending the country, fought successful wars against Egyptian invaders, worked to stop the Italian advance from Massawa and fought the Mahdists until he lost his life at the battle of Metemma in 1889. Although he had designated Ras Mengesha as his heir, it was Negus Menilek of Shewa who inherited the throne. Menilek crowned himself king of kings in 1889, and under him the old Christian kingdom grew by more than double; after the victory at Adwa in 1896 Ethiopia obtained her first internationally recognised modern boundaries. The main features of his reign were large scale territorial expansion to the south, southwest and southeast, the defence of the country by mobilising the whole population, and the modernisation begun by Tewodros.

workedExamples.problem: Why is the battle of Deresge taken as the end of the Zemene Mesafint while the battle of Ayshal is not?
workedExamples.given: At Ayshal on 29 June 1853 Kassa Hailu defeated Ras Ali Alula, ending Worashe rule, and at Deresge in February 1855 he defeated Dejach Wube of Simen and was crowned.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: the Zemene Mesafint is defined by the absence of an effective central ruler, so it ends only when a single ruler takes the throne.
workedExamples.substitution: Ayshal removed the Yejju dynasty but left Dejach Wube Haile Mariam as a powerful lord, while Deresge removed the last obstacle.
workedExamples.calculation: Only after the last rival was defeated and Kassa ascended the throne was central authority actually restored.
workedExamples.answer: Ayshal ended Worashe rule but Deresge ended the Zemene Mesafint, because only then was the last powerful lord removed and a single emperor crowned.

workedExamples.problem: Explain why the land policy of Tewodros II brought him into conflict with the Orthodox Church.
workedExamples.given: Tewodros tried to confiscate the extra land holdings of the church to redistribute them among landless peasants and declared that each church should keep only enough land for two priests and three deacons.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: reform that reduces the wealth and privilege of a powerful institution provokes resistance from that institution.
workedExamples.substitution: The church lost land and income, and the patriarch Abune Selama responded by excommunicating the emperor.
workedExamples.calculation: Because the conflict was over land and privilege, Tewodros imprisoned the patriarch in 1864 and the Abune died in prison in 1867.
workedExamples.answer: The quarrel was about church land and privilege rather than doctrine, and it turned the clergy into an opponent of the emperor.

workedExamples.problem: Compare the ways Tewodros II and Yohannis IV tried to hold Ethiopia together.
workedExamples.given: Tewodros appointed his own men in the regions he incorporated, while Yohannis granted a great deal of autonomy and did not interfere in the internal affairs of vassals who recognised him and paid tribute.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: a ruler may unify a state through direct central control or through a looser arrangement based on overlordship.
workedExamples.substitution: Tewodros chose centralisation, whereas Yohannis followed an administration that resembled federalism.
workedExamples.calculation: Centralisation provoked the regional lords who had lost power, while the looser system kept the vassals loyal for longer.
workedExamples.answer: Tewodros tried to hold Ethiopia together by centralisation and regional appointees, while Yohannis IV shared power and allowed internal autonomy in return for tribute and recognition.

workedExamples.problem: Why did the British expedition of 1868 succeed against Tewodros II?
workedExamples.given: By 1867 the army of Tewodros had declined to between 5,000 and 10,000 men, while the British force numbered 32,000 to 40,000 and had marked superiority in training and firearms.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: military outcomes depend on numbers, training, discipline and the quality of weapons.
workedExamples.substitution: The British were far more numerous, and the Ethiopian army had been weakened and divided by earlier campaigns and desertions.
workedExamples.calculation: At Arogee on 10 April 1868 the British routed the Ethiopians, killed Fitawrari Gebreye and then stormed Meqdela.
workedExamples.answer: The British won because of far greater numbers, better training and better weapons, and because Tewodros had lost the support of many lords and soldiers.

g12-history-uh3-t2.summary: The Zemene Mesafint, from 1769 to 1855, was a time of weak central power, dominant Yejju lords, regional doctrinal disputes in the Orthodox Church and great suffering for the peasants. Kassa Hailu ended it by defeating his rivals at Guramba, Gorgora Bichen, Ayshal and Deresge, and ruled as Tewodros II, whose reforms, church conflict and death at Meqdela in 1868 left a model of unity for his successors. Yohannis IV ruled from 1872 to 1889 through a liberal, federal like administration, and after his death at Metemma the political centre moved to Shewa under Menilek II, who doubled the size of the Christian kingdom and won internationally recognised boundaries after Adwa.

g12-history-uh3-t3.overview: Under Menilek of Shewa the old Christian kingdom more than doubled in size as armies and peaceful submissions brought the south, southwest and southeast under the empire. This lesson follows the three phases of expansion, the resistance of Arsi, Harar, Wolaita and Kafa, and the different land tenure systems of north and south.
objectives: Explain the reasons for Menilek's territorial expansion into the south and southwest
Describe the three phases of the expansion and the areas incorporated
Compare the peaceful submission of southwestern rulers with the resistance of Arsi, Wolaita and Kafa
Explain the main features of the northern land tenure system
Describe how the qelad system changed land holding in the south
g12-history-uh3-t3.simple: Menilek of Shewa expanded the empire in three phases between 1870 and 1900, driven by the natural wealth and trade of the south and southwest. He first brought the Oromo clans of Shewa and the Kistane Gurage under his rule, and after defeating Negus Tekle Haimanot of Gojjam at Embabo on 6 June 1882 he received the peaceful submission of Jimma, Leqa Qellem and Leqa Neqamte between 1882 and 1884. The Arsi Oromo resisted until the battle of Azule in 1886, Harar fell at Chelenqo on 6 January 1887, Wolaita under Kawo Tona was subdued in 1894 and Kafa was incorporated after Adwa. In the north the rist and gult systems kept communal land holding, but in the south the qelad system turned peasants into insecure tenants.
g12-history-uh3-t3.detailed:
Expansion was not new. Territorial expansion by the kings of the central highland kingdom was common even in the medieval period; for example, King Amde Tsion had embarked on a major territorial expansion. Menilek, however, went further than any monarch before him in incorporating the southern, southwestern and southeastern territories of present day Ethiopia. The south held the commodities of the export trade, such as ivory, gold, civet, coffee and even slaves, and Menilek also wanted to control the long distance trade of the south and southwest. To realise his aim of extending into this fertile region he worked to improve the quantity and quality of his weaponry.

The three phases. Menilek's expansion had three phases. The first covered the years from 1870 to 1889. The second was conducted between 1889 and 1896, and the last stage between 1896 and 1900. He began while he was king of Shewa in the 1870s, and the first to be incorporated in the early 1870s were the Oromo clans of Shewa.

Gurage and the battle of Embabo. The forces of Shewa then received the peaceful submission of the Kistane Gurage, who were predominantly Christians, while the southern Gurage gave stiff resistance under their leader Hassan Enjamo of the Qebena people and were subdued by the forces of Ras Gobena Dache only in 1888 after ten years of resistance. Southwestern Ethiopia was a bone of contention between Negus Menilek of Shewa and Negus Tekle Haimanot of Gojjam. At the battle of Embabo on 6 June 1882 the forces of Menilek defeated Haimanot, and this victory opened the way for expansion to the southwest.

Peaceful submission in the southwest. After Embabo the local rulers of the five Oromo kingdoms in the Gibe region and of the Leqa states in Wollega were persuaded to accept peaceful submission and incorporation into the Shewan kingdom. In return Menilek recognised the internal administrative autonomy of these kingdoms. King Aba Jifar of Jimma, Jote Tulu of Leqa Qellem and Kumsa Moreda of Leqa Neqamte were among the rulers who submitted peacefully between 1882 and 1884.

Resistance in Arsi, Harar, Wolaita and Kafa. The Arsi Oromo gave the Shewan forces very stiff resistance; six campaigns failed before the Arsi were defeated in 1886 at the battle of Azule after four years of brave fighting, the Shewan forces being led by Ras Darge, the uncle of Menilek, with Ras Gobena Dache as a commander. Unlike the southwestern rulers, the Arsi rulers were removed from their positions and replaced by governors appointed by the Shewans. Arsi was a stepping stone to the Emirate of Harar, which was subdued at Chelenqo on 6 January 1887 after a bloody battle between the armies of Menilek and Emir Abdulahi. This victory gave Menilek control of the commercial town of Harar and of the long distance trade route. After the incorporation of Harar in 1887 Menilek did not launch further campaigns until the Wolaita campaign of 1894, mainly because of the Great Famine of 1888 to 1892 known as Kefu Qen. The campaign for Wolaita was probably the bloodiest of all, and Menelik personally took part; the Wolaita people, organised under their king Kawo Tona, fought for a long time until Kawo Tona was wounded and captured and became a prisoner for the rest of his life. The kingdom of Kafa was incorporated after Ethiopia's victory over the Italians, and its people, led by their monarch Tato Gaki Sherecho, stood firm until he too was wounded, captured and imprisoned for life. In the post Adwa period Menelik also incorporated Beni Shangul, Gambella, Borena and much of the Ogaden, partly to check the advance of the European colonial powers.

How the newly incorporated regions were treated. The rulers of newly incorporated regions were sometimes used in later campaigns. In the incorporation of the Sheikhdoms of Assosa, Beni Shangul and Khomosha, Dejach Jote Tulu of Qellem and Dejach Kumsa Moreda of Neqamte gave military support to Ras Mekonnen, and the defection of Sheikh Abdurrahman Hojele to Ras Mekonnen broke the united resistance of the local people. After incorporation, Menilek reinstated loyal rulers to power as vassals; those who submitted peacefully were allowed to remain as local rulers, while those who resisted were dismissed and much land was alienated.

Land tenure in the north and the south. Northern and southern Ethiopia had different land tenure systems, especially after the nineteenth century. In the north the traditional community system of land ownership continued. Provinces such as Tigray, Begemder, Gojjam, Wollo and northern Shewa had communal land ownership, and anyone who could prove a blood connection to the landowner or the original possessor, or who had created the first settlement, could claim land. Most northern land was therefore based on the rist system, the hereditary right to hold and use land. The gult system gave the right to collect tax, and at the beginning gult rights were not hereditary. The gebbar system was the basic means by which the feudal class took surplus: a gebbar was a land holding peasant who had to pay giber, or tribute, to the state, often in kind or through unpaid forced labour for the bale gult or Melkegna. Gradually gult rights became hereditary and the riste-gult system emerged. In the newly incorporated south, peasants were gradually alienated from their land, beginning with the qelad system of land measurement. The qelad system allowed the central government to take much land, increased state revenue by classifying land tax according to fertility, and reduced the status of peasants from land owning farmers to insecure tenants on their own land; poor peasants unable to buy land were forced to migrate to towns in search of work.

g12-history-uh3-t4.overview: Egypt, Italy and the Mahdists tested Ethiopian independence in the 1870s and 1880s. This lesson follows the battles of Gundet and Gura, the Hewett Treaty, the Dogali incident and the death of Yohannis IV at Metemma, then traces the diplomatic road that led to the battle of Adwa.
objectives: Explain the causes of the Egyptian war of aggression against Ethiopia in the 1870s
Describe the battles of Gundet and Gura and their results
Explain the Hewett Treaty of 1884 and how Britain failed to honour it
Describe the Dogali incident and the mission of Gerald Portal
Explain the causes and results of the battle of Metemma
g12-history-uh3-t4.simple: In the 1870s and 1880s Ethiopia faced Egyptian, Italian and Mahdist threats. In 1875 Khedive Ismael Pasha attacked from three directions, but Emperor Yohannis IV won complete victories at Gundet on 16 November 1875 and at Gura between 7 and 9 March 1876, though the Egyptians stayed in the lands they had occupied. In the Hewett Treaty of 1884 Britain promised the return of Bogos and a free Massawa but failed to keep its word and allowed Italy to occupy Massawa. Ras Alula destroyed an Italian force at Dogali on 26 January 1887, and the envoy Gerald Portal failed to obtain an apology. Yohannis IV died of wounds at the battle of Metemma on 9 March 1889, and the way was opened for the Treaty of Wuchale and the battle of Adwa.
g12-history-uh3-t4.detailed:
Tewodros and the external challenge. In order to modernise Ethiopia Tewodros II sought the technological assistance of European nations. The lack of a positive reply from the British government prompted him to detain the British consul and other Europeans, and this led to the British military expedition against him, which ended with the storming and plundering of Meqdela. After the release of the European captives the British forces withdrew from Ethiopia. In 1875 Egypt's ruler, Khedive Ismael Pasha, launched a war of aggression on Ethiopia from three directions. In October 1875 one invading force led by Mohammed Rauf Pasha occupied Harar. Another group led by Werner Muzinger, a Swiss mercenary and the main architect of the aggression, tried to enter through Tajura but was ambushed and destroyed with his army of about 500 men by the Afar people. A third, well armed army under the Danish colonel Arendrup marched inland from Massawa and reached the Mereb River in October 1875. Emperor Yohannis IV issued a mobilisation order, crossed the Mereb River with an army of 20,000 to 25,000 and fought the Egyptians at the battle of Gundet on 16 November 1875. After two hours of effective attack the Ethiopians won a complete victory, and Colonel Arendrup with about 1,320 Egyptian troops were killed.

The battle of Gura and its results. Although Gundet was a humiliating defeat, the Egyptians did not withdraw from Ethiopian territory. In 1876 about 15,000 well armed Egyptian troops under Mohammed Ratib Pasha and the American officer General Loring invaded the north, and the second battle was fought between 7 and 9 March 1876 at Gura, in what is now Akale Guzay in Eritrea. The Ethiopians captured 2,500 Egyptian soldiers and enormous quantities of weapons. Yet the victories were not rewarding: the Egyptians remained in control of the territories they had occupied and no lasting peace treaty followed, and Yohannis IV was neither able nor prepared to push them out of Massawa or Bogos. The defeats did teach Khedive Ismael that he could not annex Ethiopian territory by force of arms, and they hastened his downfall; the guns captured from the Egyptians also helped Yohannis establish his supremacy over the other regional lords.

The Hewett Treaty of 1884 and the Dogali incident. In 1884 Emperor Yohannis IV and the British representative Admiral William Hewett signed the Hewett, or Adwa, Treaty. Yohannis agreed to help the safe evacuation of the Egyptian troops trapped in eastern Sudan through Ethiopia, and in return the British promised to ensure the return of Bogos to Ethiopia and to make Massawa a free port. Yohannis kept his word by sending his general Ras Alula Engeda to help the evacuation, but the British failed to keep their promises and instead allowed Italy to occupy Massawa. In 1885 Italy, with British help, occupied Massawa and began to expand inland, which brought it into conflict with Yohannis IV and Ras Alula, the governor of the Mereb Melash region. On 26 January 1887 Ras Alula intercepted and destroyed an Italian army of about 500 soldiers at Dogali as it moved to reinforce the Italian fortress at Saati. Dogali was the first serious blow to the Italian colonial advance and the place where the Italians suffered their first defeat by Ethiopian forces. Italy demanded an official apology and the right to occupy Keren, Assaurta and the Habab regions, and the incident provoked a strong Italian desire for revenge.

The Portal mission and the march to Saati. While Italy wanted military revenge, Britain intervened as a peace broker. The British envoy Gerald Portal met Yohannis IV in November 1887 and proposed an official Ethiopian apology for Ras Alula's attack on the Italians, which Ethiopia found totally unacceptable. Yohannis declared that he chose war rather than accept these terms, so the Portal mission failed and Ethiopia began preparations for the inevitable war. In March 1888 Yohannis mobilised a large army of 80,000 soldiers and marched to Saati, which the Italians had reoccupied, but he returned without fighting because the Italians refused to come out of their fort and fight in the open. He was also insecure about his rear because of Mahdist incursions into Gondar and the plotting of his disobedient vassals, Negus Menilek of Shewa and Negus Teklehaimanot of Gojjam.

The battle of Metemma. In the late 1880s Yohannis IV faced a triangular problem: Mahdist soldiers advanced from the west, slaughtering people, demolishing churches and monasteries and setting fire to Gondar; the Italians held Massawa, Wia and Saati; and his two vassals in the south were disobeying him. He returned to Debre Tabor in July 1888, conducted a devastating punitive campaign in Gojjam, where Tekle Haimanot submitted peacefully, and then moved towards Shewa to punish Menilek, who was being encouraged and armed by the Italians. Yohannis realised that a war with a fellow Ethiopian would only help Ethiopia's foreign enemies, and when Menilek asked for reconciliation and promised to submit, he turned to strike the Mahdists first. On 9 March 1889 the Ethiopian forces under Yohannis and the Mahdist troops, or Ansars, fought at the battle of Metemma. Despite their initial success the Ethiopians lost the battle because Yohannis was fatally wounded, and he died the next day. The battle caused a dynastic shift of power from the Tigrean house to Shewa, and the absence of strong defence in the north gave Italy a golden opportunity to advance into the Mereb Melash, which it proclaimed the Italian colony of Eritrea on 1 January 1890.

Religious policy and the Council of Boru Meda. Most Ethiopian Christian monarchs believed that religious uniformity would bring national unity, and Yohannis IV made such an attempt at the Council of Boru Meda in 1878, where he gave the Muslims of Wollo the choice of converting to Orthodox Christianity or losing their property and land. Some Wollo Muslims were baptised, while others resisted under leaders such as Sheikh Telha; the two rival chiefs Imam Mohammed Ali and Imam Amede Liben were baptised as Ras Mikael and Dejazmach Haile Mariam and were allowed to rule their parts of Wollo under the overall authority of Negus Menilek of Shewa. The same council was used to end the doctrinal controversies within the Orthodox Church, for the emperor ordered all Orthodox Christians to follow only the Tewahedo doctrine.

The road to Adwa. Menilek's relations with Italy began in 1876 with the arrival of the Italian Geographical Society in Shewa under Marquis Orazio Antinori, and continued with treaties in 1883 and 1887, and finally with the controversial Treaty of Wuchale of 2 May 1889. Article 3 gave a legal basis for the Italian colonisation of Eritrea, while the Italian version of Article 17 claimed that Menilek had to conduct all his foreign contacts through the Italian government, which reduced Ethiopia to the status of an Italian protectorate. When Menilek wrote to England and Germany he was told to write only through his protector, Italy. Menilek protested in his famous circular of 1891 to the European governments, the Tigrean princes under Ras Mengesha Yohannis swore the Mereb Convention of 6 December 1891 with Italy, and in February 1893 Menilek unilaterally abrogated Article 17, with Empress Taytu playing an instrumental role. In June 1894 Ras Mengesha and his followers submitted to Menilek, and a serious revolt broke out in Akale Guzay led by Dejach Bahta Hagos, so the Italians went ahead with their plan to conquer the whole of Ethiopia.

workedExamples.problem: Why did the brilliant victories of Gundet and Gura not bring lasting benefit to Ethiopia?
workedExamples.given: The Ethiopians won both battles, yet the Egyptians remained in control of the territories they had occupied and no lasting peace treaty followed.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: a military victory produces political results only when it is turned into a settlement or a permanent change on the ground.
workedExamples.substitution: Yohannis IV was neither able nor prepared to push the Egyptians out of Massawa or Bogos after the battles.
workedExamples.calculation: Because the occupied ports and districts were not recovered and no treaty fixed the outcome, the battlefield success changed little politically.
workedExamples.answer: The battles showed that Egypt could not annex Ethiopia by force, but without pushing the Egyptians out or signing a lasting treaty, Ethiopia gained little territory or security.

workedExamples.problem: Explain why the Hewett Treaty of 1884 is said to have worked against Ethiopia.
workedExamples.given: Yohannis IV kept his promise to help evacuate the trapped Egyptian troops, but Britain failed to return Bogos or make Massawa a free port and instead allowed Italy to occupy Massawa.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: a treaty is only as valuable as the willingness of the parties to carry out its terms.
workedExamples.substitution: Ethiopia performed its obligation, while Britain broke its promises and used the withdrawal of Egypt to open the way for Italy.
workedExamples.calculation: Because Massawa passed to Italy rather than remaining a free port, the treaty left Ethiopia facing a new colonial threat on the coast.
workedExamples.answer: Ethiopia honoured the treaty but Britain did not, and Italy's occupation of Massawa created the very danger the treaty was meant to remove.

workedExamples.problem: Explain the causes and results of the battle of Metemma.
workedExamples.given: Yohannis IV faced Mahdist attacks from the west, Italian occupation in the north and disobedience from Menilek and Teklehaimanot in the south, and he chose to strike the Mahdists first.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: fighting on several fronts at once stretches the resources of any state.
workedExamples.substitution: Because the Italian front and the vassals could not be settled at once, the emperor postponed them and marched to Metemma to deal with the Mahdists.
workedExamples.calculation: Although the Ethiopian forces had initial success, Yohannis was fatally wounded and died the next day, so the victory turned into defeat.
workedExamples.answer: At Metemma on 9 March 1889 the Ethiopians lost because Yohannis IV was fatally wounded; the result was a shift of power to Shewa and an easier Italian advance into the Mereb Melash.

workedExamples.problem: Why did the Italian version of Article 17 of the Treaty of Wuchale lead to war?
workedExamples.given: The Amharic version said Menilek may use the services of the Italian government in dealings with foreign powers, while the Italian version said he had to conduct all foreign contacts through Italy.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: a disputed text between two versions of a treaty can become a cause of war when one version limits sovereignty.
workedExamples.substitution: The Italian version turned Ethiopia into a protectorate, and Menilek was told to write to other governments only through Italy.
workedExamples.calculation: Since Menilek had not agreed to lose control of his foreign relations, he protested in his circular of 1891 and abrogated the article in February 1893.
workedExamples.answer: The Italian version reduced Ethiopia to a protectorate, so Menilek rejected it, abrogated Article 17 and prepared for the war that ended at Adwa.

g12-history-uh3-t4.summary: In the 1870s and 1880s Egypt, Italy and the Mahdists threatened Ethiopia. Yohannis IV won at Gundet on 16 November 1875 and at Gura in March 1876, but the Egyptians kept the lands they had occupied, and the Hewett Treaty of 1884 left Massawa in Italian hands. Ras Alula destroyed an Italian force at Dogali on 26 January 1887, the Portal mission failed, and Yohannis IV died of wounds at Metemma on 9 March 1889. The dynastic shift to Shewa and the disputed Italian version of Article 17 of the Treaty of Wuchale then set the stage for the battle of Adwa.

g12-history-uh3-t5.overview: The Adwa campaign of 1895 to 1896 ended in the decisive Ethiopian victory of 1 March 1896. This lesson follows the phases of the campaign and the battle, the settlement with Italy, and the national and international significance of the victory.
objectives: Describe the three phases of the Adwa campaign
Explain how the Ethiopian forces won the battle of 1 March 1896
State the terms of the Treaty of Addis Ababa of 1896
Explain the internal significance of the victory for Ethiopia
Explain the international significance of Adwa for Africa and black peoples
g12-history-uh3-t5.simple: Adwa is the collective name for a campaign that began in 1895 and ended with the main battle of 1 March 1896. It had three phases: the battle of Ambalage on 7 December 1895, the siege of Mekelle from 7 to 21 January and the final battle of Adwa. About 100,000 Ethiopians fought, nearly three quarters with modern rifles, and they defeated the Italians, who lost about 7,000 men, with 2,500 wounded and 3,500 captured. Italy signed a peace treaty in Addis Ababa on 26 October 1896 which declared the Treaty of Wuchale null and void and recognised the Italian colony of Eritrea. Internally Adwa guaranteed Ethiopian independence and an internationally recognised boundary; abroad it restored black dignity and inspired Pan-Africanism, Ethiopianism and Rastafarianism.
g12-history-uh3-t5.detailed:
The campaign. Adwa is the collective name given to a campaign that began in 1895 and ended with the main battle of 1 March 1896. The campaign had three phases: the battle of Ambalage on 7 December 1895, the siege of Mekelle from 7 to 21 January, and the final battle of Adwa on 1 March 1896. At Ambalage the Ethiopian forces led by Fitawrari Gebeyehu routed the Italian troops. The Italians then fortified themselves at Mekelle, where the forces of Etege Taytu laid siege and forced them to surrender by gaining control of the stream from which the Italians used to fetch water. Menilek surprisingly allowed the surrendered Italian soldiers to go north and rejoin their compatriots.

The battle of Adwa. At Adwa a fierce battle was fought and the Ethiopians scored a major victory over the Italians on 1 March 1896. Ethiopians from every corner of the country took part and fought the common enemy together, irrespective of their ethnic, religious and political differences. Emperor Menelik II and Etege Tayitu personally took part, and prominent war leaders such as Ras Mekonnen, Fitawrari Gebeyehu, Ras Mikael, Negus Teklehaimanot, Ras Wolle Bitul, Ras Mengesha Atikem and Dejach Balcha joined the campaign, together with Ras Mengesha Yohannes and Ras Alula Engda of Tigray and leaders of the newly incorporated territories such as King Abba Jifar II of Jimma, Kawo Tona of Wolaita and Dejach Jote Tulu of Leqqa Qellem. These leaders mobilised their forces and accompanied Menelik as far as Woreilu, where they were given a royal order to return and guard the Ethiopian frontiers. The defection from the Italian camp of the two Tigrian collaborators Ras Sibhat Aregawi and Dajach Hagos Teferi in February 1896 enabled the Ethiopian side to acquire valuable information about the Italians, while the Italians were given wrong information about the Ethiopian forces.

Forces and losses. The number of Ethiopian forces who took part in the Adwa campaign was about 100,000, of whom nearly three quarters were armed with modern rifles. In the final battle of 1 March 1896 the Ethiopians fought bravely and scored a resounding victory. The Italians lost about 7,000 of their men, 2,500 were badly wounded and 3,500 were captured as prisoners of war. After the defeat General Baratieri, the Italian governor of Eritrea, ordered a general retreat; of the three generals who led the Italian brigades, General Arimondi and General Dabormida lost their lives while General Albertone was captured.

The peace settlement. The Italian dream of reducing Ethiopia to a colony ended in failure, and Italy was left only with control over Eritrea. Italy was forced to sign a peace treaty with Ethiopia on 26 October 1896 in Addis Ababa. The Treaty of Addis Ababa declared the Treaty of Wuchale null and void, and Emperor Menelik II formally recognised the Italian colony of Eritrea. Italy became the first European state to officially recognise the independence of Ethiopia minus Eritrea without any reservation.

The internal significance. Internally the victory of Adwa guaranteed the political independence of Ethiopia, although Eritrea remained under Italian control until 1941. Adwa enabled Ethiopia to be the sole independent African country whose independence was recognised by the colonial powers in the era of colonialism, and it allowed Ethiopia to forge its own destiny free from colonial rule. It had a far reaching impact on the political economy of Ethiopia and on the psychology of the people, for it showed that if Ethiopians were united they would be strong and invincible. Even those who had grievances against Emperor Menilek II were not reluctant to die for Ethiopia.

The international significance. In Italy the humiliating defeat led to the resignation of the Italian Prime Minister Crispi. The victory was crucial not only for Ethiopia but also for the peoples of Africa and black peoples of African descent in countries such as the United States and South Africa. It restored black dignity and pride and taught a vital lesson, that black people are not inferior to white people. Adwa contributed to the birth and development of black movements such as Pan-Africanism, Ethiopianism and Rastafarianism, and it gave a powerful impetus to the anti-colonial and anti-imperialist struggle of peoples who were under the yoke of colonialism.

The boundary treaties. Adwa also enabled Ethiopia to have an internationally recognised boundary, and Emperor Menelik II signed several boundary delimitation agreements with the neighbouring colonial powers. Ethiopia signed an agreement with French Somaliland, now Djibouti, in March 1897; with the Italian colony of Eritrea in July 1900, 1902 and 1908; with the Anglo-Egyptian Sudan in May 1902; with British East Africa or Kenya in December 1907; and with Italian Somaliland in May 1908. These treaties were not followed by boundary demarcation, and they are still sources of conflict.

workedExamples.given: The campaign began in 1895 and ended on 1 March 1896, and it had three phases: Ambalage, the siege of Mekelle and the final battle of Adwa.

workedExamples.substitution: Adwa showed that a European colonial army could be defeated, which restored black dignity and pride.
workedExamples.calculation: Because it disproved the claim of white invincibility, it encouraged anti-colonial struggle and the growth of black movements.

g12-history-uh3-t6.overview: After 1906 illness, succession disputes and rival elites pulled the Ethiopian state in different directions. This lesson follows the fall of Taytu, the rule and removal of Lij Iyasu, the diarchy of Zewditu and Teferi, and the rise of Haile Selassie I to autocratic power by 1930.
objectives: Explain why the succession question became urgent after 1906
Describe the measures Menilek took to avert political chaos
Assess the reforms, strengths and weaknesses of Lij Iyasu
Explain how and why Lij Iyasu was removed from power in 1916
Describe the diarchy and the rise of Teferi to the imperial throne
g12-history-uh3-t6.simple: The year 1906 was a turning point: Menilek II suffered his first stroke, his cousin Ras Mekonnen died, and Britain, France and Italy signed the Tripartite Treaty. Menilek set up the first Council of Ministers in 1907 and named his grandson Lej Iyasu as successor in 1909, with Ras Tesema Nadew as regent, but Etege Taytu held power until the Shewan nobility and the Mehal Sefari forced her out in 1910. Lij Iyasu ruled from 1911 to 1916, introduced reforms such as the Terenbule police and a Department of Education, but his religious policy and his foreign and internal alliances turned the nobility and the colonial powers against him. He was deposed on 27 September 1916, Zewditu became Empress and Teferi regent, and after the diarchy and the battle of Anchim of 31 March 1930 Teferi took the throne as Haile Selassie I.
g12-history-uh3-t6.detailed:
The problem of succession. The year 1906 was an important landmark in the reign of Emperor Menilek II. In that year he suffered the first stroke that eventually claimed his life in 1913, and in the same year his cousin and most probable successor, Ras Mekonnen, passed away. The question of succession to the imperial throne therefore became very important. It was also in 1906 that Britain, France and Italy concluded the so-called Tripartite Treaty in an attempt to safeguard their territorial interests in the Horn of Africa in the case of succession strife in Ethiopia after the death of Menilek, who had no officially designated heir.

Menilek's measures. Although his health was deteriorating, Menilek took measures to avert possible political chaos. In October 1907 he established the first Council of Ministers in the history of Ethiopia. In May 1909 he officially designated his grandson Lej Iyasu, then only twelve years old, as his legal successor to the imperial throne, and Ras Tesema Nadew, the governor of Illubabor, was promoted to the rank of Ras Bitwoded and made the regent of Lej Iyasu.

The fall of Etege Taytu. The designation of Lej Iyasu was not welcomed by Etege Taytu, the influential wife of Menilek, who employed a skillful policy of marriage alliances to strengthen her power; her most significant arrangement was the marriage of her nephew Ras Gugsa to Menilek's daughter Zewditu. Although Iyasu was officially designated in 1909, Taytu continued to exercise supreme power, and this provoked opposition from the Shewan nobility headed by Ras Bitwoded Tesema Nadew and Fitawrari Habte Giorgis Dinegde, and also from Ras Mikael of Wollo, the father of Lej Iyasu. Fitawrari Habte Giorgis Dinegde, who had a key role in inciting the army known as the Mehal Sefari against Taytu, led the coup of 1910, which effectively removed her from the imperial court. In 1910 Taytu was forced to leave the palace and retire to Entoto, where she died in 1918.

The rule of Lij Iyasu. The removal of Taytu was followed by a reshuffling of political power in favour of the Shewan nobility, but the regent Tesema Nadew died in April 1911 and Iyasu refused to accept a new regent, so the teenager exercised full political power from 1911 to 1916, though he was never officially crowned even after the death of Menelik in 1913. The only serious challenge came from Ras Abate Buayalew, who reportedly tried unsuccessfully to break into the palace; possible bloodshed was avoided by the intervention of the patriarch Abune Mathewos. Although young and without the required experience, Lij Iyasu introduced significant social and economic reforms. He tried to give Ethiopian Muslims equal status by integrating them into his administrative hierarchy, gave financial support for the establishment of mosques and made marriage alliances with local Muslim notables. He introduced a system of auditing government property, formed a municipal police force known as Terenbule, established a separate Department of Education, took measures against the Quragngna system by which the accused and the accuser were chained together until justice was served, and tried to do away with the unfair traditional practice of thief detection called Leba Shay.

Iyasu's religious policy and his opponents. Iyasu's period became very controversial because of his religious policy, which his internal and foreign adversaries used to remove him from power. What he tried to do was to introduce an equitable system in which Christians and Muslims would live as equal citizens; he did not give special favour to Islam over Christianity and continued to build churches and give endowments to churches and monasteries. He was nevertheless charged with immorality and irresponsible leadership because he built a polygamous family, showed disrespect for the old nobility and was often absent from Addis Ababa. He also antagonised the Shewan nobility by promoting relatives and allies: in 1914 he crowned his father Ras Mikael Negus of Tigray and Wollo, took the governorship of Sidamo from Dejach Balcha Safo and gave it to his ally and brother in law Negadras Haile Giorgis, and removed Dejach Teferi Mekonnen from his family fief of Harar and transferred him to Kafa. Abroad, he antagonised Italy, France and Britain by following a pro-German and pro-Turkish policy during the First World War and by giving support to the Somali nationalist leader Sayyid Mohammed Abdullah Hassen, who was fighting the British and Italian colonisers.

The fall of Lij Iyasu. Britain, France and Italy sent a joint note to the Shewan nobility in September 1916 asking for the removal of Lej Iyasu, and the Mehal Sefari also stood against him. While Iyasu was on his usual tour of the Ogaden, his opponents assembled in Addis Ababa and convinced Abune Mathewos to excommunicate him; the coup was approved by both the Abun and the Echege, and on 27 September 1916 Lej Iyasu was deposed. Zewditu Menilek was named Empress and Dejach Teferi Mekonnen was named Ras and heir to the throne. Negus Mikael, the father of Iyasu, tried to alter the situation by leading a large army from Dessie to Shewa. Although his forces scored an initial victory at the battle of Tora Mesk, they were completely defeated and Mikael himself was captured at the decisive and bloody battle of Segele, near the town of Sheno, fought on 27 October 1916. Iyasu remained a fugitive until he was captured in Tigray in 1921, escaped from prison in 1932 with the help of Ras Hailu of Gojjam, and after being recaptured was confined at Garamuleta in Hararghe until his death in 1936.

The diarchy and the rise of Teferi. The battle of Segele restored Shewan political supremacy and began the diarchy of 1916 to 1930, in which Zewditu and Teferi theoretically ruled together but Teferi's power grew year by year while Zewditu became increasingly powerless. Teferi was more ambitious, enlightened and determined than Zewditu, who had the support of the Shewan nobility and of the traditionalists headed by Fitawrari Habte Giorgis Dinegde. In 1918 Teferi removed all the old ministers except Habte Giorgis, and in 1926 Abune Matewos and Habte Giorgis passed away. In 1928 Teferi outmanoeuvred Dejach Balcha Safo, who had rebelled in support of Zewditu, and took over his rich province of Sidamo, while Dejach Aba Weqaw, who also rebelled, was imprisoned; in October 1928 the Mehal Sefari pressed Zewditu to crown Teferi Negus. The last formidable foe was Zewditu's husband, Ras Gugsa Wole, who was defeated and killed at the battle of Anchim on 31 March 1930, where aircraft was used for the first time in Ethiopia in warfare. Two days later Zewditu died and Teferi assumed the throne as Emperor Haile Selassie I. He was crowned in a lavish ceremony on 2 November 1930 and immediately began to lay the groundwork for an absolutist state, beginning with the 1931 constitution, which helped him strengthen his power by removing hereditary rulers; in 1932 Ras Hailu of Gojjam was removed and imprisoned, and the following year the kingdom of Jimma came under complete central government control. In the military sphere the Imperial Bodyguard was established in 1930 with the help of Belgian advisors and the Holeta Military Academy was set up in 1934, until these developments were interrupted by the Italian Fascist invasion of 1935.

workedExamples.substitution: Each event removed an obstacle and added to his authority, moving him from heir to king and then to emperor.

g12-history-uh3-t6.summary: After 1906 illness, the death of Ras Mekonnen and the Tripartite Treaty made the succession question urgent, and Menilek responded with the Council of Ministers in 1907 and the designation of Lij Iyasu in 1909. Etege Taytu was forced from power in 1910, Iyasu ruled from 1911 to 1916 and introduced real reforms, but his religious policy, his appointments and his foreign alignments turned the Shewan nobility and the colonial powers against him, and he was deposed on 27 September 1916. The diarchy of Zewditu and Teferi followed, and after the battle of Anchim of 31 March 1930 Teferi became Emperor Haile Selassie I, crowned on 2 November 1930 and building an autocratic state from the 1931 constitution onwards.

g12-history-uh3-t7.overview: Fascist Italy invaded Ethiopia on 3 October 1935 and occupied the country for five years. This lesson follows the campaigns on the northern and southern fronts, the repressive Italian occupation, the two phases of the patriotic resistance and the liberation of Ethiopia in 1941.
objectives: Explain the causes of the Italian invasion of Ethiopia in 1935
Describe the main campaigns on the northern and southern fronts
Describe the Italian occupation and its six administrative regions
Explain the two phases of the patriotic resistance and the role of women
Explain how British and Ethiopian forces liberated Ethiopia by 1941
g12-history-uh3-t7.simple: Fascist Italy invaded Ethiopia on 3 October 1935 to avenge its defeat at Adwa and to build a new Roman empire. The Italians crossed the Mereb River, entered Mekelle on 8 November, defeated the northern front at Amba Aradom and Maychew, and under Marshal Badoglio captured Addis Ababa on 5 May 1936. Mussolini's empire was divided into six regions and the occupation lasted five years, but the patriots resisted in two phases, first conventional and then guerrilla warfare, after the Graziani massacre of February 1937. Ethiopia joined the League of Nations in 1923 but the League imposed sanctions on both sides. In June 1940 Italy entered the Second World War, Britain helped Haile Selassie and the patriots, and Addis Ababa was liberated on 6 April 1941, with the emperor returning on 5 May 1941.
g12-history-uh3-t7.detailed:
The causes and the invasion. Italy launched a war of aggression on Ethiopia on 3 October 1935 to take revenge for its humiliating defeat at Adwa in 1896. Italian colonial interest gathered new momentum after Benito Mussolini and his Fascist Party came to power in Italy in 1922, and above everything the Fascists wanted to restore the former glory of the ancient Roman empire. On 3 October 1935 Italian troops crossed the Mereb River that separated Ethiopia from the Italian colony of Eritrea, and on 8 November the Italians entered Mekelle.

The northern front. After an initial tactical retreat the Ethiopian forces tried to check the Italian advance in January 1936. Ras Kassa Hailu was assigned by Emperor Haile Selassie as the overall commander of the northern front, while Ras Emeru Haile Selassie held the Shire front, Ras Mulugeta Yegezu the Enderta front and Ras Kassa Hailu with Ras Seyoum Mengesha the Temben front. The major weakness of the Ethiopian side was a lack of coordination. The forces of Ras Kassa and Ras Seyoum fought two major battles in Tembien, the first in January and the second in February 1936, and although they could not finally check the Italians they fought with zeal and dedication. The forces of Ras Emeru in the Shire front in the west had some success, ambushing and destroying a force of Italian ascari at a place called Endabaguna, but the forces of the War Minister Ras Mulugeta were routed by the Italians at the battle of Amba Aradom, near Mekelle.

Maychew and the fall of Addis Ababa. The final battle on the northern front was fought at Maychew on 31 March 1936, with Emperor Haile Selassie I commanding the Ethiopian forces and the Imperial Bodyguard. The Italians fought from well fortified positions and had a marked superiority in the air, and despite some initial success the Ethiopian forces were eventually defeated. The defeat was followed by merciless aerial bombardment of the retreating Ethiopian troops. On 5 May 1936 the Italian troops headed by Marshal Badoglio captured Addis Ababa. On the southern and southeastern fronts, Ras Desta Damtew, Dejach Nesibu Zamanuel and Dejach Mekonnen Endalkachew commanded the Ethiopian forces against the Italians led by Marshal Rodolfo Graziani, who had complete control of the air and numerical superiority; a few days after Badoglio reached Addis Ababa, Graziani arrived in Harar. Ethiopia had joined the League of Nations in 1923, and although Emperor Haile Selassie went to Geneva to appeal for support, the League imposed sanctions on both the victim Ethiopia and the aggressor Italy.

The Italian occupation. The Italian forces under Marshal Badoglio entered Addis Ababa against a background of total anarchy following the flight of Emperor Haile Selassie I. Badoglio was the first Italian viceroy of Ethiopia, but he was soon replaced by Marshal Rodolfo Graziani, who served until an assassination attempt by Moges Asgedom and Abraha Deboch on 19 February 1937. Tens of thousands of innocent civilians in and around Addis Ababa were then mercilessly massacred, and soon after Graziani was replaced by the more liberal viceroy, the Duke of Aosta, who remained until the final defeat and expulsion of the Italians in 1941. The five year occupation was largely confined to the major towns because of the nationwide patriotic resistance, and it left traces in Addis Ababa, Gondar, Dessie, Harar and Jimma. The name Ethiopia was abandoned and the country became part of the Italian East African Empire together with Eritrea and Somaliland, divided into six administrative regions: Eritrea including Tigray with its capital at Asmara, Amhara including Begemder, Wollo, Gojjam and North Shewa with Gondar, Oromo-Sidama with Jimma, Addis Ababa later renamed Shewa, Harar, and Italian Somaliland including the Ogaden with Mogadishu. The occupation was marked by large scale road building, the expansion of motor transport and Italian control of the import and export trade.

The first phase of the patriotic resistance. Although the Italians defeated the Ethiopian forces in conventional warfare and occupied Addis Ababa on 5 May 1936, they faced a nationwide patriotic resistance. The resistance could be divided into two phases. The first was a continuation of the 1935 to 1936 Italo-Ethiopian War and was characterised by conventional fighting. Among its highlights was the resistance waged by three commanders of the southern front, Ras Desta Damtew, Dejach Beyene Merid and Dejach Gebre Mariam Gari, and this phase ended with the capture and execution of Ras Desta Damtew in February 1937. Another example was the ill coordinated and unsuccessful assault on the Italians in Addis Ababa in the summer of 1936, attempted by the two sons of Ras Kassa, Asfawosen and Abera, Dejach Balcha Safo, Balambaras Abebe Aregay and Dejach Fekre Mariam Yennadu, with Abune Petros as the spirit behind the offensive; Abune Petros was executed and became a martyr of the resistance, and the two sons of Ras Kassa were persuaded to surrender through the Italian collaborator Ras Hailu Teklehaimanot and were then executed.

The second phase and the collaborators. The second phase, which was largely guerrilla warfare, began soon after the Italians entered Addis Ababa and became very strong after the Graziani massacre of 1937. The February 1937 massacre was a signal for a reign of terror unleashed by the Fascist Black Shirts, whose special targets were educated Ethiopians, while the Orthodox clergy also became major victims; many churches and monasteries were burned and numerous monks of the ancient monastery of Debre Libanos were murdered, since Mussolini had ordered the execution of all monks without distinction. The resistance was especially strong in Gojjam, Begemder and Shewa, but there was no part of Ethiopia where the Italians ruled without problems, and Ethiopians of every ethnic and religious background fought the invading forces until 1941. There were also Ethiopians who helped the Italians against their own country, and these were known as banda; they created more problems for the patriots than the Italians themselves. The main collaborator was Ras Hailu Teklehaimanot of Gojjam, and others included Ras Seyoum Mengesha of Tigray, Ras Getachew Abate of Shewa, Dejach Ayalew Birru of Semen and Aba Jobir of Jimma, while Dejach Haile Selassie Gugsa of Tigray had already deserted to the Italians at the beginning of the invasion and gave them vital intelligence about Ethiopian military positions.

The liberation of 1941 and the women patriots. The outbreak of the Second World War and Italy's entry into the war on the side of Germany in June 1940 ended Ethiopia's international isolation, and Britain decided to help Emperor Haile Selassie and the Ethiopian patriots, mainly because its own colonies of Kenya, Sudan and British Somaliland were threatened by the Italian occupation. The British launched three major offensives against the Italians, two from Sudan and one from Kenya. Emperor Haile Selassie was brought from England to the Sudan and, accompanied by Brigadier General Dan Sandford and Major Orde Wingate, who led the Gedeon force, crossed the Ethiopian boundary at Omedla in Gojjam. Another British force led by William Platt defeated the Italians in Eritrea and entered Asmara in April 1941, and the British forces from Kenya under General Allen Cunningham liberated Addis Ababa on 6 April 1941. On 5 May 1941 Emperor Haile Selassie returned to Addis Ababa. Women also played a key role in the resistance struggle of 1936 to 1941. Among them were Kebedech Seyoum, Shewanesh Abrha, Lekyelesh Beyan and Senedu Gebru; they collected wood, fetched water, prepared food for the combatants and took care of the wounded, encouraged brave fighters and some took part in actual combat. Some women served as Inner Patriots, officially within the Italian camp but secretly helping the patriots with information, provisions, arms, ammunition and medicine, such as Woyzero Shewareged Gedle of Shewa, who played an important part in the patriotic attack on the Italian garrison at Addis Alem sixty kilometres west of Addis Ababa, and Woyzero Shewanesh Abebe of Gondar, who used her good command of Italian to provide valuable information.

workedExamples.problem: Why did the Italians defeat the Ethiopian forces in 1936 when they had failed so badly in 1896?
workedExamples.given: In 1936 the Italians had complete control of the air, numerical superiority on all fronts and modern weapons, while the Ethiopian side lacked coordination and faced aerial bombardment.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: military outcomes change with technology, supply and organisation, not with courage alone.
workedExamples.substitution: At Adwa in 1896 the Ethiopians were united, well armed and better informed, while in 1936 the Italians used aircraft and modern equipment against forces that could not coordinate.
workedExamples.calculation: Air power and coordination allowed the Italians to break the fronts one by one, so the same enemy that failed in 1896 succeeded in 1936.
workedExamples.answer: Italy won in 1936 because of air supremacy, superior numbers and equipment, while the Ethiopian side suffered from poor coordination and relentless aerial attack.

workedExamples.problem: Explain why the Italian occupation was largely confined to the major towns.
workedExamples.given: The occupation lasted five years, but it left traces mainly in Addis Ababa, Gondar, Dessie, Harar and Jimma because of the nationwide patriotic resistance.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: an occupying power cannot control a large country if the rural population keeps fighting.
workedExamples.substitution: Patriots operated across almost all provinces and made lasting control of the countryside impossible.
workedExamples.calculation: Because the Italians could not secure the interior, their rule was concentrated in towns that they could garrison and supply.
workedExamples.answer: The occupation was confined to the towns because the nationwide patriotic resistance, especially the guerrilla struggle, made control of the countryside impossible.

workedExamples.problem: Explain the difference between the two phases of the patriotic resistance.
workedExamples.given: The first phase was a continuation of the 1935 to 1936 war and was characterised by conventional fighting; the February massacre of 1937 began the second phase, which was characterised by guerrilla warfare.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: the form of a resistance struggle changes according to the strength of the enemy and the lessons of earlier defeats.
workedExamples.substitution: After the defeat of the regular armies, the patriots could no longer fight open battles, so they turned to small scale attacks and concealment.
workedExamples.calculation: The Graziani massacre confirmed the brutality of the occupier and pushed survivors into the guerrilla warfare of the second phase.
workedExamples.answer: The first phase used conventional fighting until Ras Desta Damtew was executed in February 1937, while the second phase after the Graziani massacre used guerrilla warfare until 1941.

workedExamples.problem: How did the outbreak of the Second World War change the struggle for liberation?
workedExamples.given: Italy entered the Second World War on the side of Germany in June 1940, and the British colonies of Kenya, Sudan and British Somaliland were threatened by the Italian occupation of Ethiopia.
workedExamples.formula: Historical concept: a local struggle can be transformed when a wider war brings new allies and new resources.
workedExamples.substitution: Because Britain now needed to defeat Italy, it decided to help Haile Selassie and the Ethiopian patriots, and it brought the emperor from England to the Sudan.
workedExamples.calculation: With British troops, the Gedeon force and the patriots fighting together, the Italians were defeated and Addis Ababa was liberated on 6 April 1941.
workedExamples.answer: The world war ended Ethiopia's isolation, brought Britain in as an ally, and the combined British and patriotic forces expelled the Italians by 1941.

commonMistakes: Thinking the Italian occupation lasted only a few months, when it lasted five years, from 1936 to 1941.
Believing the occupation covered the whole country evenly, when it was largely confined to the major towns because of the patriotic resistance.
Confusing the first phase of the resistance, which was conventional, with the second phase, which was guerrilla warfare after the massacre of February 1937.
Thinking all Ethiopians supported the patriots, when some, known as banda, helped the Italians.
Forgetting that Ras Desta Damtew was captured and executed in February 1937.
Believing the League of Nations helped Ethiopia, when it imposed sanctions on both the victim and the aggressor.
Thinking the British forces acted alone in 1941, when the Ethiopian patriots also fought both before and during the liberation.

The Italian East African Empire was divided into six regions and the occupation lasted five years, largely confined to the towns. The patriots resisted in two phases, first conventional fighting and then guerrilla warfare after the Graziani massacre of February 1937, in which women and Inner Patriots played a key part. After Italy entered the Second World War in June 1940, British forces and the Ethiopian patriots defeated the Italians, liberated Addis Ababa on 6 April 1941, and Haile Selassie returned on 5 May 1941.
